title: AV-FlowEdit and QSTar Interaction in Audio-Visual Reasoning
summary: AV-FlowEdit introduces a training-free, inversion-free framework for audio-visual editing, leveraging event-aware spectral trajectory preservation to preserve structure and cross-modal coherence. QSTar enhances audio-visual understanding by integrating query-guided spatial-temporal-frequencies, improving performance on AVQA benchmarks.

facts.statement: AV-FlowEdit enables prompt-driven audio-visual editing without requiring model training or optimization.
QSTar combines query-guided interaction with frequency-domain characteristics of audio signals to enhance audio-visual understanding.
Experiments show significant improvements in both performance and quality across AVQA benchmarks.

sources.title: AV-FlowEdit: Training-Free Prompt-Driven Audio-Visual Editing with Event-Aware Spectral Trajectory Preservation
sources.description:
arXiv:2610.13072v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Joint audio-video diffusion models generate synchronized content, but editing existing clips requires target changes without disrupting non-target structure or cross-modal correspondence. We present AV-FlowEdit, a training-free and inversion-free framework for prompt-driven audio-video editing. Our key insight is that source--target flow differences provide both cross-modal editing directions and preservation cues. Under shared perturbations, they jointly update the video and audio branches, supporting visual-only, audio-only, and joint edits while retaining pretrained cross-modal interactions. To suppress drift accumulated during sampling, Cross-Modal Event-Aware Spectral Trajectory Preservation combines flow saliency, aligned audio activity, multiscale low-frequency displacement, and diffusion-stage scheduling. This adaptively preserves unsupported regions while allowing intended audio-visual events. AV-FlowEdit requires no model training, external masks, or optimization-based inversion. Experiments show strong prompt alignment and temporal consistency, together with competitive audio quality and cross-modal coherence.

sources.title: Query-Guided Spatial-Temporal-Frequency Interaction for Music Audio-Visual Question Answering
sources.description:
arXiv:2601.19821v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Audio--Visual Question Answering (AVQA) is a challenging multimodal task that requires jointly reasoning over audio, visual, and textual information in a given video to answer natural language questions. Inspired by recent advances in Video QA, many existing AVQA approaches primarily focus on visual information processing, leveraging pre-trained models to extract object-level and motion-level representations. However, in those methods, the audio input is primarily treated as complementary to video analysis, and the textual question information contributes minimally to audio--visual understanding, as it is typically integrated only in the final stages of reasoning. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Query-guided Spatial--Temporal--Frequency (QSTar) interaction method, which effectively incorporates question-guided clues and exploits the distinctive frequency-domain characteristics of audio signals, alongside spatial and temporal perception, to enhance audio--visual understanding. Furthermore, we introduce a Query Context Reasoning (QCR) block inspired by prompting, which guides the model to focus more precisely on semantically relevant audio and visual features. Extensive experiments conducted on two AVQA benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method, achieving significant performance improvements over existing Audio QA, Visual QA, Video QA, and AVQA approaches. The code is released under https://github.com/lik1996/QSTar.

sources.title: A Systematic Study of Cross-Modal Typographic Attacks on Audio-Visual Reasoning
sources.description:
arXiv:2604.03995v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As audio-visual multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, understanding their cross-modal vulnerabilities is essential. To this end, we introduce Multi-Modal Typography, a systematic study examining how perturbations added to speech and on-screen text impact audio-visual reasoning of closed- and open-source models. For instance, on the WorldSense benchmark, the attack success rate (ASR) against Gemini 3.7 Flash increased from 9.53\% to 43.41\%, highlighting its vulnerability. We analyze the cross-modal effects of unimodal and multimodal attacks and evaluate how specific properties of the attacks impact the overall multi-modal reasoning. By applying fine-tuning as a mitigation, we lower the ASR of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B on WorldSense from $60.6\%$ to $52.0\%$. Our findings across multi-modal reasoning tasks, content moderation, and offline robot task selection benchmarks establish multi-modal typography as a critical and underexplored attack strategy in multi-modal reasoning. Code and data will be made publicly available.
